title: Amycretin: Dual GLP-1/Amylin Agonist — Research Dossier
excerpt: Amycretin is Novo Nordisk’s novel unimolecular dual GLP-1 and amylin receptor agonist now in Phase 3 development. Phase 1b/2a data published in The Lancet (2025) showed up to 22% weight loss over 36 weeks. This dossier covers its mechanism, clinical data, oral formulation progress, and research limitations.
content:
Research compounds discussed for educational purposes. Not FDA-approved for human use where applicable. Consult a healthcare provider before use.

What Is Amycretin?

Amycretin (NN9487) is a novel investigational compound developed by Novo Nordisk that simultaneously activates both GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) and amylin receptors through a single unimolecular design. Unlike combination therapies that deliver two separate agents, amycretin covalently links a GLP-1 analog and an amylin analog into one molecule, enabling coordinated dual-pathway signaling from a single injection or oral dose.

While semaglutide and other GLP-1 receptor agonists act only on GLP-1 pathways, amycretin adds amylin receptor activation — a complementary satiety mechanism centered in the brainstem. The hypothesis is that two pathways working in concert may produce additive or synergistic effects on appetite suppression, gastric emptying, and metabolic regulation beyond what either pathway achieves alone.

Mechanism of Action

Amycretin operates through two distinct but complementary satiety pathways:

  • GLP-1 receptor activation: Stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and reduces food intake via hypothalamic appetite centers. This is the same mechanism as semaglutide and other approved GLP-1 receptor agonists.
  • Amylin receptor activation: Amylin is a 37-amino-acid peptide hormone co-secreted with insulin by pancreatic beta cells. It acts primarily in the brainstem (area postrema, nucleus tractus solitarius) to suppress post-meal glucagon, slow gastric emptying through a pathway independent of GLP-1, and reduce food intake through distinct neural circuits. The only approved amylin mimetic, pramlintide, demonstrated additive weight loss when combined with insulin.

The oral formulation uses SNAC (salcaprozate sodium) as a permeation enhancer to facilitate intestinal absorption — the same technology underlying oral semaglutide (Rybelsus), which made the first approved oral GLP-1 peptide commercially viable.

Key Research Findings

Subcutaneous Phase 1b/2a Trial

The core efficacy data come from a Phase 1b/2a dose-escalation trial (NCT06064006) published in The Lancet in 2025 (Dahl et al.):

  • Design: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; adults with overweight or obesity (BMI ≥27 kg/m²)
  • Dose range: 0.3 mg to 20 mg weekly subcutaneous injection
  • Primary endpoint: percent change in body weight
  • At 20 mg (highest dose), 36 weeks: approximately 22% mean body weight reduction
  • Placebo: approximately 1.1% weight change
  • Weight loss trajectory had not plateaued at 36 weeks
  • A higher-dose analysis reports up to 24.3% weight reduction

Oral Phase 1 First-in-Human Trial

A Phase 1 oral trial (NCT05369390) was published in The Lancet in 2025 (Gasiorek et al.):

  • Highest dose tested: 2×50 mg daily
  • 13.1% mean body weight reduction over 12 weeks versus 1.1% on placebo
  • Weight loss still progressing at 12 weeks (no plateau observed)
  • This is a first-in-human trial; confirmatory Phase 3 oral data are pending

Type 2 Diabetes Phase 2

A Phase 2 trial in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight/obesity reported up to 14.5% weight loss over 36 weeks at subcutaneous dosing, alongside significant HbA1c reductions.

Phase 3 Development Status (as of October 2026)

Novo Nordisk announced in June 2025 that both subcutaneous and oral formulations will advance into Phase 3 development, with program initiation planned for Q1 2026 in adults with overweight or obesity. Phase 3 efficacy and safety results are not yet available.

Dosing in Research

Subcutaneous doses in trials: 0.3 mg – 20 mg weekly. Oral doses tested: up to 2×50 mg daily. These are investigational doses used in controlled clinical trials and do not represent approved, prescribable, or safe dosing regimens for human use outside of trials. Amycretin is not approved anywhere as of October 2026 and is available only within authorized clinical trials.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does amycretin differ from semaglutide for weight loss?

Amycretin activates two separate satiety pathways — GLP-1 and amylin receptors — while semaglutide targets only GLP-1. Phase 1b/2a data showed approximately 22% weight loss at 36 weeks, which appears to exceed the approximately 15% seen with semaglutide at comparable timepoints in Phase 2/3 trials. However, no direct head-to-head trial has been published as of 2026, so cross-trial comparisons are confounded by different patient populations and study designs.

Is there an oral form of amycretin in development?

Yes. Oral amycretin showed 13.1% weight loss over 12 weeks in its Phase 1 first-in-human trial, with weight still declining at the 12-week endpoint. Novo Nordisk announced both subcutaneous and oral formulations will enter Phase 3 development starting Q1 2026. An effective oral GLP-1/amylin dual agonist would represent a major advance in convenience over injectable therapies.

What side effects appeared in amycretin clinical trials?

Side effects were consistent with the GLP-1 drug class: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring most frequently during dose escalation phases. These are dose-dependent and typically moderate in severity. Serious adverse event rates and full discontinuation data are available in the primary Lancet publications (Dahl et al. and Gasiorek et al., 2025).

Research Limitations

  • All published efficacy data are from Phase 1 and Phase 2 trials; Phase 3 results are not yet available
  • Long-term safety data beyond 36 weeks are limited
  • No published head-to-head comparison with semaglutide or tirzepatide
  • Most trials enrolled adults with overweight or obesity (BMI ≥27–30 kg/m²); efficacy in normal-weight or elderly populations is unstudied
  • Oral bioavailability and long-term oral tolerability require Phase 3 confirmation
  • The additive vs. synergistic nature of the dual agonism has not been mechanistically confirmed in humans
